source_refs.note: Topic 7.2.3, printed pages 148-150 (Figures 7.3 and 7.4 are photographs, not reproduced).

blocks.text: The change in concentration of reactants or products can be determined by chemical or physical methods, depending on the substances involved.

This suits reactions in solution: a reactant or product is analysed chemically. The acid hydrolysis of an ester such as ethyl acetate with a small amount of acid is one of the best examples: CH3COOC2H5 + H2O, with H+ as catalyst, gives CH3COOH + C2H5OH. The ester in water and the acid catalyst are allowed to react; after some time a sample is withdrawn with a pipette and run into about four times its volume of ice-cold water, the dilution and chilling stopping the reaction. The acid formed is titrated against a standard alkali such as NaOH with phenolphthalein as indicator. Repeating the analysis at various times gives the change in the concentration of acetic acid during the reaction.

items: Spectrophotometry or colorimetry: applicable when a reactant or product absorbs ultraviolet, visible or infrared radiation; the rate is followed by measuring the radiation absorbed, as for a coloured reaction mixture.

Electrical conductivity: for reactions involving ions, the conductivity of the solution depends on the changing concentration of the reacting ions or the ions formed, and is proportional to the rate of change of their concentration.

Volume change: for reactions that change the volume of a gas, the volume change is directly proportional to the extent of reaction and the change in concentration, as when a gas given off is collected.

blocks.alt: (a) Six test tubes in a rack, samples taken every 2 minutes from 0 to 10, their colour fading from dark red to pale yellow as the coloured reactant is used up. (b) A colorimeter: light from a lamp passes through a filter and a cuvette of the sample to a detector, and a meter shows the absorbance. A note says deeper colour absorbs more light, so readings at regular times show how fast the concentration changes.
blocks.caption: A colour change followed by colorimetry (original diagram after Figure 7.3).

blocks.alt: A stoppered conical flask holds a reaction mixture giving off gas bubbles. A delivery tube leads from the stopper to a horizontal gas syringe, marked 0 to 100 cm3, clamped to a stand; its plunger is pushed out as gas collects. A note says to read the volume every 30 s with a stopwatch, since the volume of gas against time gives the rate.
blocks.caption: Following a reaction rate by the volume of gas given off (original diagram after Figure 7.4).

blocks.title: Interesting information
blocks.text: Very fast reactions can be followed by stopped-flow spectrophotometry: small volumes of reactants are driven at high speed into a mixing chamber and on to an observation cell, where the progress of the reaction is monitored, usually by the transmission of ultraviolet radiation, and a graph of rate against time is generated automatically.

blocks.prompt: Which method would you choose to follow each of these, and why: marble chips reacting with hydrochloric acid; bromine water fading as it reacts with an alkene; a reaction that produces ions from neutral molecules?
blocks.explanation: Marble and acid give off carbon dioxide, so collect the gas and follow the volume change. Bromine water is coloured and the product is not, so use colorimetry to follow the fading. A reaction producing ions raises the conductivity of the solution, so follow it with the electrical conductivity method.

items: Chemical method: withdraw samples, quench by dilution and chilling, titrate (ester hydrolysis, acid titrated with NaOH and phenolphthalein).
Physical methods: colorimetry (absorbed radiation), electrical conductivity (ions), volume change (gases); stopped-flow spectrophotometry for very fast reactions.
